opening.headline: Even in services believed to have a no-data-retention agreement, could data still be retained due to abuse monitoring?
body: API providers classify usage logs to detect policy violations and may also separately record suspicious requests. These records are stored in a layer independent of the path that generates service responses. Therefore, it is difficult to conclude that data is not retained merely because the non-persistent option has been applied.

In this lesson, we compare abuse monitoring documentation from three providers, examine logs that developers enable directly and their shared options. We then review a table distinguishing retention periods and access subjects, and summarize how to map out retention layers using a diagram.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain abuse monitoring retention and logging policies
Data retention periods and access subjects can be distinguished by data layer.

screens.title: Data may be stored separately due to misuse monitoring.
screens.lead: This is a case of a service that handles sensitive inquiries via an API, under the belief that a no-data-retention contract has been established. Please read it while considering where the data flows.

visual.alt: Diagram showing an API request splitting into response path and monitoring path, with a "stored" indication applied to the monitoring path.

paragraphs: A customer believes they have entered a no-retention agreement and submits a sensitive inquiry via the API. Looking only at the response path, it appears as though the request is processed and a response is returned, with nothing remaining afterward.

However, providers may run classifiers to detect policy violations and keep separate records of certain prompts. These records are stored in a layer separate from the service response pathway. The retention period and entities authorized to access them vary depending on the provider and the type of contract.

This course's question is: Which data remains accessible where, to how many people, and to whom? Reporting only that data is checked at one location without storage leads to overlooking critical layers.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Misuse monitoring is a procedure for detecting policy violations, while non-persistence is a commitment regarding whether data is stored after a response. The two settings are distinct.

screens.outro: First, let's recall what we know about abuse monitoring.

screens.title: Review the scope of data retained by misuse monitoring
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please try answering it yourself before clicking.

items.prompt: Do you know that the original prompt can appear in abuse monitoring logs?
items.answer: OpenAI's documentation states that this log may contain customer content such as prompts and responses. If you thought the log contained only summaries or statistics, you may have underestimated the scope of what is being stored.

items.prompt: Have you confirmed in the documentation who can view this log?
items.answer: Retention period is just as important as access control. Google Docs explains that classified prompts are reviewed by authorized staff. It's necessary to develop the habit of separately verifying both retention period and access control.

items.prompt: Do you consider non-preservation agreements and misuse monitoring to be the same setting?
items.answer: They are not the same. Non-storage is a commitment regarding whether data is stored after a response, while misuse monitoring is a procedure for detecting policy violations. How these two interact depends on the provider and the type of contract.

screens.outro: We will compare documents individually by provider.

screens.title: Misuse monitoring documentation from three providers
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare, by provider, what is stored and for how long, and which customers are affected.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: Abuse monitoring logs are generated whenever any API feature is used, and by default, these logs are retained for up to 30 days. Exceptions apply when legal requirements mandate longer retention or when threat mitigation is necessary. These logs may include metadata derived from content, such as prompts, responses, and classifier outputs. Approved customers may exclude customer content from logs using Modified Abuse Monitoring or ZDR.

tabs.label: Google
tabs.body: When an automated classifier detects suspicious activity, it logs the prompt solely for the purpose of investigating policy violations. This data is not used for model training and is stored for up to 90 days in the region selected by the customer, where it can be reviewed by authorized personnel. The logs are protected under Google Cloud's guarantees, such as data residency location assurances, but are not encrypted using the customer's management encryption keys. This applies to customers whose accounts are governed by Google Cloud terms; Cloud Master Agreement customers are excluded by default from this logging.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body: Under ZDR, responses are returned without storing the prompt or response. Data retention is specified on a per-feature basis and follows the principle of retaining only as much data as is necessary. However, it is noted that content flagged by legal requirements or safety systems, even when no retention or HIPAA settings are configured, may be retained for up to two years.

screens.outro: In addition to monitoring, there are logs that developers directly enable, so let's proceed to examine the logging policy further.

screens.title: Log policy: Developer-owned logs and shared options
screens.lead: Compare how the purpose of data usage and the subjects who access it differ when alternating between two states—logging data only versus sharing a dataset.

states.label: Log only retention
states.body: Gemini API logs are developer-owned data available only in projects where payments are enabled. These logs are accessible only within the project and are distinct from separately stored logs used for abuse monitoring. Logs are stored by default for a maximum of 55 days and can be customized to 7, 14, 28, or 55 days in AI Studio. Once the retention period expires, logs are automatically marked for deletion. During this marked-for-deletion status, prompts and responses from the logs are not used for product improvements.

states.label: Dataset sharing
states.body: When logs of interest are converted into a dataset, the predefined retention period no longer applies. Sharing this dataset with Google enables use in product improvements and model training, and allows human reviewers to examine inputs and outputs. The documentation warns against including personal information, sensitive information, or confidential information in shared logs. While sharing is optional, once logs are shared, any subsequent retention period settings no longer serve as a protective barrier. Therefore, before enabling logs or creating or sharing a dataset, it is essential to first determine what data is being fed into prompts and to verify that no sensitive information is mixed in. It is particularly important to note that logs already converted into a dataset are no longer subject to retention period settings, even if the retention period is shortened. Also remember that setting a short log retention period and deciding whether to share logs are two distinct control measures.

screens.outro: Now let's read the table that distinguishes retention periods and access subjects by data layer.

screens.title: Table distinguishing retention period and access subjects
screens.lead: The table below summarizes the retention periods and access authorities for each data layer examined so far. Please note that the retention periods and access authorities vary by layer.

data.caption: Data retention periods by data layer and access subjects
rows: The basic period is up to 30 days. It may be extended depending on legal requirements.

The document states that, depending on approval conditions, customer content may be excluded from logs or safety preservation may be applied, in which case the classifier indicates that flagged content can be reviewed by a human.
The classifier retains suspicious prompts for a maximum of 90 days.
Authorized Google employees evaluate flagged prompts.
The basic maximum is 55 days and can be adjusted to 7 days, 14 days, 28 days, or 55 days.
The project owner observes that when a dataset is shared with Google, reviewers can view it.
This document does not specify a separate access entity and should be understood as records intended for organizational auditing; access permissions must be verified separately.
Follow the organization's retention policy until the user deletes it.
It follows the policies set by the organization.
data.notes: Local session logs are stored by default for six years, but if the organization specifies a period, that period applies. The durations in the table are not comparable because they represent different types of numeric values. Some apply only to suspicious activity requests, some to logs enabled by developers, and others to organizational management records.

screens.outro: Let us extend our example to practicing reading tables.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Cases where monitoring data remains even in non-preservation contracts
screens.lead: This is the instructor's explanation after reporting that no preservation was applied. Follow the arrows step by step to locate the remaining layer.

steps.title: Verifies the sentences in the report
steps.body: The customer reported to internal audit that "no retention" was applied. To verify whether this one sentence is accurate, we must first examine the model, features, and contract type involved.

steps.title: OpenAI: The model can be exceptional
steps.body: OpenAI states that even for customers whose accounts have approved ZDR or Modified Abuse Monitoring, they may choose not to apply these options to specific models, provided they have been notified in writing beforehand. In such cases, customer content will be stored in encrypted logs. When investigating significant risks, safe custody may be applied, allowing human reviewers to examine flagged content.

steps.title: Google: The target varies depending on the contract type
steps.body: Prompt logging applies to customers whose agreements are governed by the Google Cloud Terms. In this case, classifiers have up to 90 days remaining before flagged prompts are logged. Cloud Master Agreement customers are excluded by default from this logging, resulting in different outcomes for the same service based on the applicable contract.

steps.title: Check logs by function
steps.body: There are non-extractable, function-specific logs similar to search grounding query logs, and functions that store state follow their own retention policies. You must check each function's documentation to verify whether it generates separate logs.

steps.title: Reflect the conclusion in the report.
steps.body: Instead of using the single term "no retention," it is necessary to separately specify the retained layers and durations by contract type, model, and function, as well as the access subjects to ensure accuracy. Layers that have not been verified should be left as pending verification rather than being definitively classified as "no retention."

screens.outro: Since we confirmed that there are multiple floors, let's create a map to summarize this at a glance.

screens.title: Draw the preservation layer on a map
screens.lead: The following diagram illustrates storage points on a data flow map. Select the number marker to view examples of labels that can be assigned to each point.

visual.alt: A data flow diagram showing four storage points numbered along the path from request to response.

markers.label: Our app logs
markers.title: Our application logs and monitoring tools
markers.body: Regardless of the provider's retention policy, original records may remain in our logs. Labels should specify the retention period, access authorities, and reduction methods (such as masking or log truncation). The point we control is where reduction can be applied first.

markers.label: Abuse Monitoring
markers.title: Provider Abuse Monitoring Logs
markers.body: The target varies depending on the provider and contract type. Labels should include the maximum retention period (e.g., OpenAI 30 days, Google 90 days), access authorities, and reduction options (Modified Abuse Monitoring, ZDR, contract type verification).

markers.label: Function Status
markers.title: Features stored in the state and logs
markers.body: This is data that is separated into distinct functional units, similar to files, threads, or grounding. Labels should include the TTL specified in the functional documentation, and reduction methods may involve not using the respective function. Any points not confirmed in the documentation remain pending verification.

markers.label: Developer log
markers.title: Developer's opened logs and shared dataset
markers.body: Gemini API logs retain a default maximum of 55 days and can be adjusted. When converted into a dataset, the time period is removed and becomes shareable with people. At this point, it's important to note the current value in the label since we can modify the settings accordingly.

screens.outro: This map serves as a common basis for contract review and audit reports. Now, I will summarize the entire content.

screens.title: Unified consolidation: preservation is multi-layered.
screens.lead: Let's go back to the first question and clarify it: consider why data might still remain even under a non-preservation agreement.

paragraphs: Retention is not a single setting but rather composed of multiple layers. Responses, abuse monitoring logs, state stored by features, developer-enabled logs, and our application logs are each separately retained. Retention agreements apply only to some of these.

Each floor has different retention periods and access authorities. OpenAI retains data for a maximum of 30 days by default, Google retains data for up to 90 days for suspicious prompts, and Gemini API developer logs are retained for a maximum of 55 days by default. Access authorities also vary from project owners to authorized provider employees, so both retention periods and access authorities must be verified separately.

Ultimately, the most reliable method of verification is to map out all storage points where our data passes through, and then label each point with its duration, access entities, and reduction methods.

checks.intro: Review the provider-specific documents you just compared. The results are not recorded.
checks.q: Why is it risky to write "No storage" in an internal report stating that the no-preservation option has been applied?
options: This is because no retention is always released one week later.
Because different models, contract types, and functionalities may require separate storage layers such as monitoring.
The preserve option does not actually exist.
The report does not permit the use of storage period.
checks.explain: ZDR may not apply to certain models, and prompt logging applies depending on the contract type. All remaining layers must be verified.

wrong.0: Automatic release is not contained in the document.
wrong.2: The preserve option exists but is subject to conditions on its scope.
wrong.3: It is recommended to record the storage period per floor.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Depending on the model, contract type, and features, separate storage layers may exist, so it would be risky to conclude this in a single sentence.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This reason does not match the content of the document. Please reconsider the conditions attached to the scope where the no-archival option applies.

checks.intro: Pair log types with their retention characteristics. Scores are not stored, so feel free to try.
checks.q: Pair log types with their retention characteristics.
right: Store suspicious prompts for up to 90 days in investigation mode
checks.explain: Developer logs can be retained by owners for adjustable periods, investigative prompt logging is retained for up to 90 days, and activity feeds are separately preserved for six years.
checks.correctFeedback: All three pairs match. The logs are accurately distinguished based on their different periods and purposes.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There's a mismatch somewhere. Please re-establish the connection based on whether the log is being generated by whom and for what purpose.

glossary.def: A procedure used by providers to classify and log usage records in order to detect policy violations.
Rules defining log creation, retention period, and sharing status.
The period during which data remains before it is deleted.
An individual or organization authorized to view stored data.
OpenAI's option to exclude customer content from misuse monitoring logs.

misconceptions.myth: If no logging is preserved, no logs remain.
misconceptions.fact: Monitoring logs or feature logs may be generated depending on the model, contract type, and features. They must be verified layer by layer.

misconceptions.myth: Monitoring logs are used for model training.
misconceptions.fact: Google documents state that these records are not used for model training. However, the retention period and access rights must be verified separately.

misconceptions.myth: Our logs don't need to be concerned about.
misconceptions.fact: If the original text is retained in our application logs, that location becomes a retention site regardless of the provider's non-retention policy.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Retention is composed of multiple layers.
Misuse monitoring logs are verified independently of the no-retention agreement.
Distinguishes storage periods by layer and access subjects.
Displays all storage locations in the data flow diagram.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are intended for you to think about on your own and are not submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: When we list all the storage points that our data passes through, where is the location still unverified?
